title: The Open Source AI Stack
gist: Together AI's Hassan El Mghari lays out the 'MIGHT' stack (Model, Inference, Gateways, Harness, Tools) as five decoupled, swappable layers of open-source agentic AI coding, arguing the real edge in 2026 is composability and disciplined model/context selection, not committing to any single vendor's bundled AI coding product.

themes.theme: The MIGHT stack: five decoupled layers

insights.claim: The open-source AI coding stack decomposes into five independent layers: the model (interprets requests), inference (infrastructure/provider running it), gateways/routers (route requests across providers by cost/speed/capability), the harness (manages the conversation and gives the model tools), and tools via skills and MCP (task-specific knowledge and context access).
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating AI-infra vendors should map them to a specific layer (model, inference, gateway, harness, or tools) rather than treating 'AI coding platform' as one undifferentiated category — each layer has different competitive dynamics.
insights.locator: The MIGHT Stack

insights.claim: Because the five stack layers are independent, developers can swap any single layer — most often the model — in minutes without rebuilding the rest of their workflow, which lowers the switching cost every time a new model ships.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Low switching costs at the model layer compress any single model vendor's pricing power and shorten the half-life of a 'best model' lead — favors infra/gateway players over any one model lab.
insights.locator: These layers are all independent from one another

insights.claim: Developers already comfortable operating Claude Code are functionally close to being able to use open-weight models, since the application-developer experience (a model plus a harness) is nearly identical across closed and open ecosystems.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Low behavioral switching cost from closed to open models is a demand-side tailwind for open-model inference providers and a competitive risk to closed-model vendors' lock-in.
insights.quote: If you already know how to use Claude Code, you’re much closer to using open models than you probably think.
insights.locator: If you already know how to use Claude Code

insights.claim: Most leading open models are now Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures that contain many specialized experts but activate only a small subset per token, letting them carry larger total parameter counts while needing less compute per generated token.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: MoE's compute-per-token advantage is the mechanism behind falling open-model inference cost curves — a structural tailwind for inference-provider unit economics.
insights.quote: Most leading open models are now Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) models that contain many specialized “experts”, but only activate a small subset of them for each token generation.
insights.locator: Models come in a range of sizes

insights.claim: Kimi K3, cited as an example large open model, has 1.8 trillion total parameters and 104 billion active parameters, and is positioned for complex, ambiguous, multi-step tasks like refactoring an authentication system or debugging why a SQL database suddenly slowed down.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Concrete active/total parameter figures for a leading open MoE model are a reference point for estimating its inference cost versus dense large models.
insights.locator: A good example of a large open model is Kimi K3

insights.claim: GLM 5.3 Flash, cited as an example small open model, has 320 billion total parameters and 18 billion active parameters, making it roughly 6 times smaller and about 20 times cheaper than Kimi K3 while remaining strong on narrowly-scoped, well-specified coding tasks.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: A ~20x cost gap between a 'small' and 'large' open frontier model quantifies how much margin is available to whoever correctly routes tasks to the cheaper model.
insights.locator: An example of a small open model is GLM 5.3 Flash

insights.claim: The dividing line between large and small open models is less about raw quality and more about how much task ambiguity they can absorb: large models excel at under-specified, multi-step work, while small models match large-model quality once a task is explicit and tightly scoped.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Teams that invest in tightening task specs (prompts/workflows) can shift more volume to cheap small models — a controllable lever for cutting AI-coding inference spend.
insights.locator: The difference between small and large is less about quality

insights.claim: Model selection should be treated like picking the right tool from a toolbox for a given task rather than crowning one 'winner' model, since a larger model that solves a problem more reliably is often several times slower and more expensive than a smaller one that would do the same one-file change correctly.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Portfolio-style multi-model routing, not single-model procurement, is the efficient-frontier strategy for AI-coding cost/quality — relevant to how enterprises should structure inference spend.
insights.quote: Rather than thinking of bigger models as being better than smaller models, it’s better to think of these models as two different types of tools in a toolbox.
insights.locator: Models as tools

insights.claim: Leaderboards such as The Open Frontier and Artificial Analysis are useful for discovering available open models and getting a rough comparative sense of intelligence, coding ability, speed and price, but should not be over-relied on since benchmark scores compress behavior that a specific real workload may not reflect.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Investors and teams benchmarking AI-coding vendors should discount pure leaderboard rank and weight task-specific evals more heavily — a warning against index-style model selection.
insights.quote: Do not spend too much time trying to identify the single best model on a leaderboard.
insights.locator: Picking the model

insights.claim: As of this piece, the most popular open models cited are GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Kimi K3, and MiniMax M3, though the author notes this set changes very rapidly.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: A named snapshot of the current open-model leaderboard as of September 2026 — useful as a dated reference point given how fast rankings turn over.
insights.locator: For reference, the most popular open models

themes.theme: Inference providers and the commoditized model layer

insights.claim: Two different inference providers running the same open model, at the same version and sampling settings, should generally produce similar output quality; provider differentiation instead shows up in price, latency and API features, meaning the underlying open model itself is a largely commoditized input.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: If open-model quality is commoditized across providers, competitive advantage and margin for inference vendors accrue from price/latency/API execution, not model exclusivity — key for valuing inference-provider businesses like Together AI versus closed-model labs.
insights.quote: Two providers running the same model should generally produce similar results, especially when you use the same model version and sampling settings.
insights.locator: Inference providers

insights.claim: Together AI is cited as an example cloud inference provider offering a large catalog of both large and small open models accessible from a single account, positioning cloud providers as the easiest on-ramp for experimenting with new open models via simple API key access.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Breadth of model catalog under one account is a concrete competitive lever for inference providers competing for developer adoption.
insights.locator: Providers such as Together AI and others

insights.claim: Because open models are not hosted uniformly across every inference provider, no single provider account can access every model, which creates structural demand for a gateway/router aggregation layer sitting above individual providers.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Fragmented model-to-provider coverage is the underlying demand driver for gateway businesses like OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway — a distinct, addressable layer of the stack.
insights.locator: Gateways and routers

themes.theme: Gateways, routers, and bridging closed harnesses to open models

insights.claim: Cloud gateways such as OpenRouter and the Vercel AI Gateway sit in front of multiple inference providers and aggregate them behind a single API, letting developers route requests across backends, compare pricing and latency, and switch models without changing application code.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Gateways are a distinct monetizable layer (aggregation/routing) separate from both model labs and raw inference hosting — worth tracking as its own competitive category.
insights.locator: A gateway sits in front of multiple inference providers

insights.claim: As an alternative to cloud gateways, developers can self-host routing with tools like LiteLLM, giving a single local API endpoint that routes across multiple already-configured provider accounts.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Self-hosted routing is a lower-lock-in substitute for commercial gateways — relevant for assessing gateway vendors' pricing power against a free/open alternative.
insights.locator: You can also run your own router locally

insights.claim: TogetherLink is presented as a way to connect closed-source harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex to open-weight models, extending open-model access to developers who don't want to switch away from a closed-source harness.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: A bridge product like TogetherLink lets an inference vendor (Together AI) capture open-model usage even from users who stay on closed-source harnesses — an adoption wedge that decouples harness choice from model-vendor lock-in.
insights.locator: For closed-source harnesses like Claude Code and Codex

themes.theme: Harnesses set agent quality as much as the model does

insights.claim: The harness is the orchestration layer that maintains conversation state and executes actions on the model's behalf (running searches, reading files, applying patches); the model decides what should happen next but never itself touches the filesystem or shell directly — the harness is what actually makes it happen.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: This division of labor is the core architectural reason harness quality is a separate value driver from model quality when evaluating AI-coding products.
insights.locator: Harnesses

insights.claim: The same underlying model can feel noticeably different across two different harnesses because harness quality depends on how well it exposes tools, collects relevant context, manages long conversations, applies patches, displays changes, asks for permission, and recovers when commands fail — so overall coding-agent quality depends on more than model choice alone.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Benchmarking 'which model is best' in isolation is misleading; investors comparing AI-coding products should evaluate harness engineering quality as a distinct, defensible moat independent of the underlying model.
insights.quote: The same model can feel noticeably different in two different harnesses.
insights.locator: A good harness knows how to expose tools

insights.claim: Named harnesses with support for open models include PI, OpenCode, and Amp, spanning terminal-based CLI harnesses, in-editor IDE extensions, and web/desktop apps, with philosophies ranging from feature-rich (integrations, background agents, project management) to minimal (just conversation, shell, and file editing).
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: A concrete, named competitive set of open-model-compatible harnesses to track for share shifts as the open-model ecosystem matures.
insights.locator: Here are a few popular harnesses with support for open models

insights.claim: Ease of switching model or provider with a single command or config change is frequently marketed as a selling point specifically of open-source harnesses, versus closed-source harnesses that need bridge tools like TogetherLink to reach open models.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Open-source harnesses are positioning switching flexibility itself as a product differentiator against closed-source incumbents — a go-to-market angle to watch.
insights.locator: Most harnesses make it easy to change from one provider

themes.theme: Extending the harness: skills and MCP

insights.claim: Skills are reusable, on-demand instruction sets that a harness loads only when needed to give the model specialized knowledge for a specific task (e.g., deploying an app, reviewing code, working with a particular framework), avoiding the need to stuff everything into one large system prompt; community skills can be discovered via skills.sh.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Skills marketplaces (e.g., skills.sh) are an emerging distribution layer for task-specific IP in the AI-coding stack, separate from model and harness vendors.
insights.locator: Skills are reusable instructions that tell a model

insights.claim: MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how agents connect to external tools and data sources (databases, APIs, filesystems, developer tools) through a common interface instead of bespoke integrations per tool; servers can be discovered via mcp.so, and providers including Together AI publish their own MCP servers.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: MCP standardization lowers integration costs across the ecosystem, which should accelerate third-party tool adoption inside AI-coding agents and favor vendors that ship first-party MCP servers.
insights.locator: MCP, short for Model Context Protocol

themes.theme: Context management and the plan-implement-review workflow

insights.claim: Long-running coding sessions accumulate files, failed approaches, and pages of test output that the model must reason through on every subsequent turn, degrading output quality even before hitting the model's hard context limit; starting a new session for each new task, or whenever switching models or reconsidering an approach, is one of the simplest ways to improve agent output.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Session-hygiene discipline is a free, immediately actionable lever for improving AI-coding agent reliability without any change in model or spend.
insights.quote: One of the simplest improvements you can make to an agent workflow is starting new threads more often.
insights.locator: New sessions

insights.claim: A recommended multi-model workflow splits work across three models by role: a large model plans by breaking an open-ended prompt into well-defined isolated tasks, a small model implements each task in its own fresh session, and a large model reviews all completed work, looping back to planning if problems surface.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: This plan/implement/review pattern is a concrete cost-optimization template — large-model spend is concentrated at planning and review, small-model spend absorbs the bulk of execution volume.
insights.locator: Plan, implement, and review

insights.claim: Within the plan-implement-review workflow, if a specific task proves too complex for the smaller implementing model, the recommendation is to escalate just that task to a larger model rather than abandoning the small-model-first approach entirely.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Task-level escalation (not wholesale model switching) is the efficient failure-handling rule for cost-optimized multi-model pipelines.
insights.locator: If any task turns out to be too complicated

themes.theme: The composability thesis and vendor lock-in

insights.claim: Because model, inference/gateway, harness, and tools are decoupled layers, a better model released next week can be swapped in without replacing any other part of the stack, undercutting the value proposition of committing to a single vendor's all-in-one AI coding product.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: This is a direct disintermediation risk to bundled, single-vendor closed AI-coding products — value migrates toward best-of-breed composable stacks, a structural argument for backing infra/tooling layers over closed all-in-one suites.
insights.quote: Instead of choosing an AI coding product, you can build your own AI coding stack.
insights.locator: The open stack

insights.claim: Open-weight models carry an additional option value beyond choosing among cloud providers: developers can self-host smaller open models entirely, for example running them locally on a laptop with tools like Ollama, removing dependence on any inference provider.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: Local-inference optionality via tools like Ollama is a ceiling on cloud inference-provider pricing power for smaller open models — a structural floor investors should factor into inference-provider margin assumptions.
insights.locator: you also have the option to take the model elsewhere

insights.claim: As a concrete worked example of a fully composable stack, the author cites OpenCode as the harness, GLM 5.3 Flash running on Together AI as the model/inference layer, custom skills for UI work, and Playwright MCP for browser automation — with no two pieces coming from the same company.
insights.speaker: Hassan El Mghari
insights.so_what: A concrete named multi-vendor reference stack for benchmarking against bundled single-vendor AI coding products on cost and flexibility.
insights.locator: For example, your coding stack could be OpenCode
